paras: The attempted lynching of Martin near Fort Hanson was a pursuit in New Mexico Territory in 1888 in which a posse chased a dentist named Martin, accused of chloroforming and raping a servant girl, intending to lynch him. Martin escaped into the Sacramento mountains, was later arrested in Arizona, and was convicted and sentenced to five years in the penitentiary.

Martin was described as a "dissolute, wandering dentist" with a wife and family at Prescott, Arizona. Some time before October 1888 he went to Fort Hanson, which the dispatch called the military post on the Mescalero Apache Reservation. Neither report gives the race of Martin or of the girl.

Martin was accused of chloroforming and "outraging" a servant girl who worked on a cattle ranch adjoining the fort. When the accusation became known he fled toward El Paso, intending, according to the dispatch, to cross the Rio Grande into Mexico. A "posse of cowboy soldiers" went after him and, in the dispatch's words, "would have lynched him if caught." He reached the Sacramento mountains, where his pursuers could not follow, and later returned to his family in Arizona.

The girl's friends then had the Sheriff of Lincoln county sent to Prescott to arrest him. Martin was tried in late September 1888, convicted, and sentenced to five years in the penitentiary; the place of trial is not stated. His wife stood by him, and after the conviction a subscription was raised to send her home to Arizona.

The story reached readers through a copyrighted California Associated Press dispatch dated El Paso, October 2, which the Sacramento Daily Record-Union printed on its front page under the headings "A Frontier Crime" and "Fiendish Act of an Arizona Dentist in New Mexico." That version called Martin "dissolute" and, in a line about his wife, her "worthless spouse," and it reported the posse's intent to lynch him as a matter of course, without comment. Ten days later the Omaha Daily Bee compressed the dispatch into two sentences among western news briefs, saying Martin had escaped "a band of lynchers." No local New Mexico report or Black-press coverage of the case was found.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Martin near Fort Hanson
bases: A posse pursued a man accused of rape and, according to the only full report, 'would have lynched him if caught', but he escaped and no one was harmed (A1, A2).

No one was killed: the accused escaped the posse into the mountains and was later tried and sentenced in court (A1, A2); the episode was an attempted lynching by a posse described as intending to lynch him for an alleged rape (A1).
Both reports are the same California Associated Press dispatch from El Paso, the Omaha Bee's a condensed version of the Record-Union's (A1, A2); no local or independent account was found.

accounts.label: Wire report (California Associated Press, El Paso)
accounts.gist: Martin chloroformed and outraged a servant girl near Fort Hanson, fled, escaped a posse of 'cowboy soldiers' who would have lynched him, returned to Arizona, and was arrested, convicted and sentenced to five years.

framing.detail: The Record-Union ran the copyrighted dispatch on page one as 'A Frontier Crime' / 'Fiendish Act of an Arizona Dentist in New Mexico', calling Martin 'dissolute' and 'worthless' and stating the posse's intent to lynch without comment.
The Omaha Bee reduced the story to one sentence-pair among western news briefs, with the posse rendered as 'a band of lynchers'.

record_check.dossier: Not stated; the offense and pursuit happened 'a short time ago' before Oct. 2, 1888, and the trial was in late September, so the pursuit may well predate September.
Inferred only from the Sheriff of Lincoln county being sent to make the arrest; no county is named for the crime scene.
Neither report gives the race of Martin or of the girl.
